title: Canadian firms see a floor under sales, with little appetite to expand payrolls
summary: Canadian firms entered 2026 expecting a modest improvement in sales after a weak year, but their hiring and investment plans gave little indication of a broad expansion. The Bank of Canada's Business Outlook Survey found less anxiety about an outright recession and few widespread constraints on production. The clearest change was that the drag from trade tensions was generally expected to stop intensifying. Firms were still making decisions under considerable uncertainty. The survey interviewed senior managers at about 100 businesses from 6 to 26 November. The accompanying monthly Business Leaders' Pulse results cover October to December and special consultations provide separate evidence on energy. Respondents' forecasts express their own judgements.

The distinction between improvement and strength is visible in the survey balances. The share of firms planning for a Canadian recession over the next year fell from 33% to 22%, its lowest reading in 2025 but still above 2024 levels. Roughly a third had experienced falling sales volumes over the preceding year, compared with a historical average of about a quarter. Chart 2's balance of firms with improving rather than deteriorating forward sales indicators rose from zero to 13 percentage points, still below the historical average of 24. The balance measures the breadth of improvement. It gives neither the implied aggregate growth rate nor the size of any individual change in sales.

Trade exposure separated businesses with quite different prospects. Firms strongly affected by US policies reported weaker past and expected sales. The damage reached beyond firms paying tariffs. Customers postponed spending, and suppliers to steel, aluminium and auto producers lost orders. Housing-related businesses also described weak household demand. Less exposed firms reported pockets of growth, for example by supplying affordable goods or serving higher-income households. Most exporters to the US said their products qualified for exemptions under the trade agreement. American customer hesitation, weak demand and the firms' own reluctance to enter the US market could nevertheless limit sales. Chart 4 shows only a small share growing sales elsewhere. Distance, regulatory requirements and specialised equipment make it costly to redirect exports, especially for firms without an established overseas customer base.

Capacity and staffing offer a test of whether a sales improvement would immediately tighten the economy. In Chart 5, 33% said they would face some or significant difficulty meeting an unexpected increase in demand, against a historical 44.4%. Labour shortages rose from 13% to 22% of respondents but remained below their 28.6% average. The share expecting to reduce staffing rose from 13% to 21%, its highest since 2016. The data do not predict a corresponding percentage decline in employment. On investment, the net balance rose from seven to 14 percentage points, close to its historical average of about 16. Yet 63% cited equipment replacement or repair as an investment purpose, compared with 41% citing expansion. These responses can overlap. A firmer aggregate investment intention can coexist with caution about building new capacity (Charts 5–8).

On pricing, several firms directly affected by trade tensions expected weaker wage increases because their profitability or performance had deteriorated. Wage expectations overall had roughly stabilised after slowing. The quarterly survey's expected wage increase over the next year was 3.3%, compared with 2.4% in the Business Leaders' Pulse series shown in Chart 9. Chart 10 shows just under 10% expecting significant input-price increases and around 6% expecting significant selling-price increases. Both were down on the previous quarter. Firms continued to cite trade costs, but switching suppliers could mitigate those pressures, and earlier tariff pass-through was no longer a source of upward pressure on pricing decisions. Commodity prices and less intense demand restraint were counterweights. Inflation expectations consequently remained around 2.5–3% across horizons rather than falling in step with the shares expecting substantial price increases (Charts 9–11).

Energy illustrates why investment spending, unit economics and output can diverge. Firms consulted expected global oversupply to keep WTI near US$60 per barrel in 2026. At that price the margin above the roughly US$57 average WTI break-even for conventional producers was narrow. Heavy-oil producers selling against WCS could curtail drilling quickly. Oil sands producers faced an estimated average break-even nearer US$50 WTI. Scale, long-lived operations, access to the Trans Mountain Expansion pipeline and a narrower price discount supported them. Staff calculations and industry estimates describe segment averages, with important variation between projects. The approximately US$12 WTI–WCS differential is a separate price spread. Participants expected it to remain near that level for one to two years. They expected Canadian natural gas at around C$2.50 per gigajoule in 2026, with new LNG export demand offering support.

Announced industry plans in Chart 1-A imply a 1.7% decline in nominal capital spending alongside a 2.6% rise in production across producers. The two bars describe expected changes in different quantities. More output from oil sands and gas, efficiency gains and export capacity can sustain production even while conventional drilling is curtailed. Producers emphasised the increase in the share of oil exports going outside the US, from under 3% to over 9%, mainly to Asia. For a portfolio exposed to Canadian growth, the report thus points to different risks for an equipment supplier, a conventional driller and an oil sands producer. It supplies neither a realised earnings outcome nor a valuation comparison among them.

questions.question: Do improving orders turn into actual hiring and capacity expansion?
questions.detail: Chart 2's forward-sales balance has turned positive while most firms expect stable or lower staffing and equipment replacement dominates spending intentions. This matters for whether stronger sales would absorb spare capacity or support substantially more household income. Track subsequent survey balances against realised hours, payrolls and business fixed investment. Distinguish replacement from expansion and examine orders by trade exposure before inferring a broad cyclical turn.

questions.question: Has tariff pass-through faded because costs fell, margins absorbed them, or demand constrained prices?
questions.detail: Fewer respondents expect large price increases and some report sourcing changes. The survey supplies no economy-wide split between lower landed costs and margin compression. Compare sectoral import and selling prices with survey comments and issuer gross margins in heavily affected sectors. The distinction matters for both the persistence of consumer disinflation and whether it comes at the expense of corporate profitability.

questions.question: Which producers could sustain their output plan if the realised oil differential widened?
questions.detail: Box 1 gives WTI assumptions, segment-average break-evens and plans for aggregate production. Individual producers' realised prices, transport commitments and reinvestment needs can differ materially. Examine producer budgets and sensitivity disclosures, pipeline flows and realised WCS differentials alongside the cited industry plans. This would help distinguish short-cycle drilling exposure from the outlook for long-lived capacity under the same benchmark oil price.
